PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Bonda, 120 children were assessed in 20 schools in Malkangiri. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to read the findings

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). Students are placed in five performance groups for each competency, L0 to L4, signifying increasing performance. For the Bonda assessment, the results available for every competency are the share of students in L4 (scoring above 75%); the bars therefore show L4 in green and the remaining students (L0 to L3 together) in grey.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 98% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 88% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 94% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 71% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 77% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 51% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 49% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 60% of the students in Bonda correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 40% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 84% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 38% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 62% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 65% of the students scored above 75%.

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 95% of students in Bonda were in the proficient group (L4), while 5% were in L0 to L3.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 59% of the students in Bonda counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 70% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 74% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

43% of the students discerned and completed more than three-quarters of the number patterns correctly.

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 45% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

Subtraction Level 2

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 57% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 43% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 31% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 32% in subtraction word problems.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Bonda

The literacy findings reveal an interesting contrast between children's relatively strong oral language and reading fluency skills and their difficulties with comprehension and written expression.

Decoding skills

The findings indicate a relative strength in oral reading fluency, with 95% of children scoring above 75%, suggesting that a large proportion can read aloud with reasonable accuracy and fluency. However, oral reading fluency needs to be interpreted alongside other decoding competencies, including phonemic awareness, letter naming fluency, word reading accuracy, word reading fluency and sentence reading. On the writing front, performance is considerably weaker: only 38% of children score above 75% in sentence writing, while 17% are zero scorers in independent writing. This suggests that the ability to reproduce or read language may not yet be translating into the ability to independently construct and express ideas in written form. Possible contributing factors include limited opportunities for regular writing practice, insufficient development of sound-letter association and spelling skills, and limited exposure to structured sentence construction activities in Bonda.

Comprehension skills

Oral language competencies emerge as a significant strength, with 98% of children scoring above 75% in oral vocabulary and 94% in listening comprehension. This indicates that children demonstrate a strong familiarity with spoken Bonda vocabulary and can understand orally presented information. However, this strength does not translate proportionately into reading comprehension, where only 60% of children score above 75%. This gap suggests that children may be able to understand language when it is spoken to them but face greater difficulty independently extracting meaning from written text. Independent writing presents an additional concern, with 17% of children unable to demonstrate success on the assessed task. The possible reasons for the comprehension gap include limited opportunities to connect decoding with meaning-making, insufficient exposure to age-appropriate reading materials in Bonda, and limited classroom emphasis on questioning, inference, retelling and discussion around texts. The comparatively weaker written expression may also indicate that children have fewer opportunities to translate their oral vocabulary and understanding into written responses.

Overall interpretation

The Bonda findings point towards a potential disconnect between oral language proficiency, reading fluency, reading comprehension and written expression. The priority should therefore be to move beyond developing the ability to read words and sentences towards building meaning-making, comprehension and independent expression.

15

Math in Bonda

The numeracy findings indicate that children demonstrate relative strengths in number identification, measurement and multiplication, but experience considerable difficulty with addition, subtraction and the application of mathematical concepts to word problems.

Foundational skills

Number identification emerges as a relative strength, with 74% reported in the timed task. The low performance in addition and subtraction suggests that children may not have developed sufficient conceptual understanding of number operations, place value and the relationship between numbers. Possible contributing factors include limited use of concrete materials for demonstrating addition and subtraction, insufficient opportunities for hands-on practice with grouping and regrouping, and an overemphasis on procedural methods rather than number sense and conceptual understanding. These gaps may also affect children's ability to progress from simple calculations to more complex operations.

Application skills

Children demonstrate relative strengths in measurement (71%) and multiplication (73%), suggesting some familiarity with these mathematical concepts and their application. However, only 31% of children score above 75% in addition word problems and 32% in subtraction word problems, indicating difficulty translating mathematical understanding into problem-solving situations. This contrast is particularly important: children may be able to recognise or perform certain mathematical operations in isolation but struggle to identify the appropriate operation when presented with a contextual problem. Possible contributing factors include limited exposure to contextualised mathematical problems, insufficient opportunities to connect mathematical concepts with everyday experiences, lack of mathematical vocabulary and difficulties interpreting the language used in word problems.

Overall interpretation

The Bonda numeracy findings suggest a need to strengthen the foundational understanding of number operations, particularly addition and subtraction, while developing children's ability to apply mathematical concepts to contextualised problems. The gap between performance in individual mathematical tasks and word problems highlights the importance of moving beyond procedural fluency towards conceptual understanding, mathematical reasoning and application in everyday contexts.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Strengthen decoding and foundational reading: Provide structured, regular practice in phonemic awareness, letter recognition, letter-sound association, word reading accuracy and fluency, and sentence reading. Use familiar Bonda words and contexts to strengthen children's ability to connect spoken language with written text.
  • Move from reading fluency to reading comprehension: Leverage children's strong oral vocabulary, listening comprehension, and oral reading fluency through shared reading, read-alouds, storytelling, retelling and sequencing activities. Gradually introduce factual and inferential questions to help children move beyond reading text to understanding it.
  • Prioritise sentence construction and independent writing: Introduce a structured progression from word writing to sentence construction and independent writing. Use picture-based prompts, familiar experiences, oral narration and guided sentence formation to help children translate their strong oral language abilities into written expression.

Numeracy

  • Reinforce foundational number sense and operations: Provide hands-on learning opportunities using locally available materials such as stones, seeds and sticks to strengthen number recognition, counting in bundles, number comparison and number patterns. Focus particularly on building conceptual understanding of addition and subtraction through concrete materials, visual representations and progressively abstract calculations.
  • Strengthen addition and subtraction through differentiated practice: Identify children struggling with addition and subtraction and provide targeted instruction using number lines, grouping, decomposition and place-value activities. Move progressively from simple calculations to more complex operations, ensuring children understand the underlying concepts rather than merely memorising procedures.
  • Connect mathematical understanding to everyday problem-solving: Use familiar Bonda contexts, such as counting collected forest produce, sharing objects, measuring quantities and handling money, to develop mathematical application. Encourage children to interpret word problems with Math vocabulary, identify relevant information, select appropriate operations and explain their reasoning.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Conduct focused classroom observations to assess how teachers are addressing comprehension, independent writing, number sense and addition-subtraction gaps. Demonstrate practical teaching strategies, examine student reading and writing samples and numeracy work, provide actionable feedback, and follow up during subsequent visits to assess improvements in classroom practice.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Review implementation of Bonda-specific academic priorities across MLE schools through regular block-level reviews. Ensure the availability of Bonda-language teaching-learning materials, teacher participation in academic support activities and regular CRCC visits, while resolving administrative barriers affecting classroom implementation.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Establish periodic district-level reviews of Bonda LFA findings and subsequent school-level progress. Set clear expectations for block officials on monitoring literacy and numeracy priorities, review evidence from school visits and mentoring records, and ensure timely administrative convergence to address gaps in teacher availability, resources and classroom support.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead the development of a Bonda-specific academic improvement strategy by analysing competency-wise learning gaps, developing contextualised teaching-learning resources and conducting focused capacity-building sessions for teachers and CRCCs on reading comprehension, independent writing, number sense and teaching addition and subtraction conceptually. Identify demonstration classrooms and use them to strengthen pedagogical practices across MLE schools.

Way Forward

Performance groups exist to show what children can do, what they are yet to learn and what support will help them progress, not simply to classify them. Teachers should use the results to plan differentiated instruction; schools and clusters can draw on them in Monthly Cluster Meetings, classroom observations and Sikhyana Sopan tracking; and the State and districts can use them to target teacher development and learning materials. Building on Bonda children’s oral language and number recognition strengths offers the most direct route to closing the gaps in comprehension, writing, operations and problem-solving.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Didayi, 81 children were assessed in 13 schools in Malkangiri. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 93% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 100% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 98% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 72% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 94% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 67% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 33% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 59% of the students in Didayi correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 41% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 94% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 67% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 33% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 76% of the students scored above 75%.

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 97% of students in Didayi were in the proficient group (L4), while 3% were in L0 to L3.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Didayi

Decoding skills

In Didayi, children show strong foundations in early sound and word-level skills. Phonological awareness is a particular strength, with 100% scoring above 75%; oral reading fluency is 97%, word reading accuracy (untimed) is 94%, and word writing is also 94%. Independent writing is 76%. However, sentence reading and sentence writing are both at 67%, indicating that strong performance at the sound, word and oral-reading levels is not yet translating consistently into reading and writing complete sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (93%) and listening comprehension (98%) are strong, while picture comprehension is 72% and reading comprehension is 59%. This pattern suggests that children understand spoken Didayi very well, but have more difficulty constructing meaning from written text and visual prompts. Independent writing is comparatively stronger at 76%, although sentence writing remains 67%. The difference may indicate that children can express ideas in some independent tasks but need further support to organise those ideas into complete written sentences.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited regular exposure to connected, age-appropriate Didayi texts; classroom practice that gives more time to sounds, words and oral reading than to sentence-level reading and discussion; and insufficient modelling of how to ask questions, infer meaning and retell a text. Children’s strong oral language and phonological awareness provide a useful base, but the bridge from oral language and word recognition to sentence-level meaning-making may need strengthening. These are hypotheses to check through classroom observation and review of student work, not established causes.

15

Math in Didayi

Foundational skills

Number identification is 74% in the untimed task and 88% in the timed task; number comparison is 82%, while counting in bundles is 66% and number patterns are 60%. Addition Level 1 is 49% and Addition Level 2 is 65%. Subtraction Level 1 is particularly low at 32%, although Subtraction Level 2 is 74%. This uneven pattern suggests that many children can recognise numbers and compare quantities, but may not consistently understand or carry out basic operations – especially subtraction – across task types.

Application skills

Children show relative strengths in measurement (90%), 2-D shape recognition (94%) and data handling (84%). Multiplication (74%) and division (71%) are developing, while money is 54%, 3-D shape recognition is 69%, and time is 42%. Application is weakest in word problems: 39% score above 75% in addition word problems and 28% in subtraction word problems. This suggests that performance on familiar or visually supported concepts is stronger than using operations to solve contextual problems, particularly subtraction situations.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited use of concrete materials and number representations to build subtraction concepts, insufficient practice explaining how an operation is chosen, and word-problem language or contexts that children may not readily connect with and lack mathematical vocabulary. Strong performance in measurement and 2-D shapes may reflect greater familiarity with visible, hands-on concepts, while time, money and 3-D shapes may require more deliberate use of real objects and practical situations. These explanations need to be checked against the actual tasks, classroom practice and children’s responses.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Use Didayi sound games, syllable segmentation and familiar-word activities to sustain the strong phonological-awareness foundation, while checking that children can connect sounds to the letters used in their learning materials.
  • Build a daily progression from fluent word reading to sentence reading: model reading a short Didayi sentence, pause to discuss its meaning, and ask children to arrange, complete or read sentences using familiar vocabulary.
  • Use short Didayi stories, picture sequences and read-alouds to strengthen picture and reading comprehension. Ask children to retell, sequence events and answer both direct and simple inferential questions; then move from oral responses to writing complete sentences.

Numeracy

  • Strengthen counting in bundles and number patterns using locally available objects. Ask children to group, regroup, compare and explain quantities, building on their stronger number identification and comparison skills.
  • Prioritise subtraction, especially Level 1, through concrete take-away and comparison situations using seeds, stones or sticks. Move from objects to drawings and number sentences, and check that children can explain what changes when quantities are taken away.
  • Teach addition and subtraction word problems through familiar Didayi contexts and Math vocabulary. Read the problem aloud, identify what is known and what is being asked, represent it with objects or drawings, choose the operation and explain the answer. Include practical activities with clocks, money and 3-D objects to address weaker areas.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • During school visits, observe whether teachers are moving beyond word-level reading and routine calculations to sentence comprehension, sentence writing and conceptual subtraction. Model a short Didayi reading-and-retelling lesson and a concrete subtraction or word-problem lesson, review children’s work, and agree on one follow-up action with each teacher.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Review MLE school-wise progress on sentence reading, reading comprehension, sentence writing, subtraction and word problems in block meetings. Ensure teachers receive Didayi reading and numeracy materials, CRCC visits take place as planned, and practical barriers such as material availability and teacher participation are resolved.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Make the Didayi learning priorities part of the district review agenda. Ask block officials to report evidence from school visits and CRCC mentoring, not only activity completion, and coordinate timely administrative support for teacher availability, learning materials and regular classroom support.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead a Didayi-focused academic response by working with language resource persons and teachers to develop short, graded Didayi texts, sentence-building and comprehension activities, and concrete subtraction and word-problem resources. Orient teachers and CRCCs on using these resources, and review student work from selected schools to refine the approach.

Way Forward

The next review should track five priority skills

sentence reading, sentence writing, reading comprehension, Subtraction Level 1 and word problems. Progress on these will show whether children are moving from strong foundations to independent reading for meaning and confident problem-solving.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Gondi, 362 children were assessed in 48 schools in Nabarangpur. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to read the findings

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). Students are placed in five performance groups for each competency, L0 to L4, signifying increasing performance. For the Gondi assessment, the results available for every competency are the share of students in L4 (scoring above 75%); the bars therefore show L4 in green and the remaining students (L0 to L3 together) in grey.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 94% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 81% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 86% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 83% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 63% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 45% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 55% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 34% of the students in Gondi correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 66% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 70% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 40% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 60% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 70% of the students scored above 75%.

12

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 72% of students in Gondi were in the proficient group (L4), while 28% were in L0 to L3.

Letter Naming and Word Reading Timed

Addition Level 1 and Subtraction Level 1 combine untimed and timed items and are shown with the accuracy tasks.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 68% of the students in Gondi counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 52% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 49% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

40% of the students discerned and completed more than three-quarters of the number patterns correctly.

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 37% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

Subtraction Level 2

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 39% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 61% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 34% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 27% in subtraction word problems.

14
Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Gondi

Decoding skills

In Gondi, children show a gap between oral language foundations and the reading skills needed to work with connected text. Phonological awareness is 81%, oral reading fluency is 72% and word reading accuracy (untimed) is 63%, while sentence reading is only 45%. Word writing and independent writing are both 70%, but sentence writing is 40%. The pattern suggests that many children are not yet consistently combining words to read or write complete sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (94%), listening comprehension (86%) and picture comprehension (83%) are relative strengths. Reading comprehension, however, is only 34%, the lowest literacy result, while independent writing is 70%. This sharp difference suggests that children may understand spoken language and visual information but struggle to access meaning independently from written text. The low sentence-reading score (45%) may be one factor limiting comprehension, as children need to read connected sentences before they can make meaning across a passage.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include insufficient guided practice in moving from word reading to sentence reading, limited access to familiar Gondi print materials, and classroom routines that may emphasise oral responses or word recognition more than reading connected text. Children may also need explicit support to connect each word in a sentence, understand how the words work together and discuss the meaning of a passage. Sentence writing may be weak because children have fewer opportunities to orally rehearse, compose and then write complete sentences. These are hypotheses, not proven causes.

15

Math in Gondi

Foundational skills

Foundational number skills are a major concern. Number identification is 52% in the untimed task and 49% in the timed task; number comparison is 63%, counting in bundles is 68% and number patterns are 40%. Addition Level 1 and Level 2 are 41% and 37%, while Subtraction Level 1 and Level 2 are 33% and 39%. These low results indicate that many children may not yet have secure number sense or reliable understanding of basic operations. The source table does not provide separate timed and untimed scores for addition and subtraction.

Application skills

Data handling (79%) is the strongest reported application skill, while 2-D shape recognition is 71%, measurement 70%, multiplication 68%, division 59%, 3-D shape recognition 61% and money 47%. Time is 32%. Word problems are particularly difficult: 34% score above 75% in addition word problems and 27% in subtraction word problems. Children may be able to work with some visual or organised information, but find it difficult to select and apply an operation in a written or spoken situation.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include gaps in number recognition and pattern understanding that make later operations harder; limited use of physical grouping and number representations; and insufficient step-by-step modelling of addition and subtraction. Word problems may also place an additional language-comprehension demand on children with a lack of Math vocabulary, especially when the wording or context is unfamiliar. Low time and money scores may reflect limited classroom opportunities to use clocks, calendars, coins and practical daily-life situations as learning resources. These possibilities should be verified through task review and classroom observation.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Rebuild the reading pathway systematically with a practice of sound awareness and letter-sound connections, then word reading, and finally short connected Gondi sentences. Use teacher modelling, echo reading and repeated reading rather than asking children to move directly from words to passages.
  • Use oral vocabulary and picture comprehension as entry points for reading comprehension. Before reading, discuss the picture and key words; during reading, pause to check meaning; after reading, ask children to retell and answer simple factual questions before moving to inferential questions.
  • Make sentence construction a daily routine. Let children describe familiar people, objects and events orally, arrange word cards into sentences, complete sentence frames and gradually write their own sentences. Review whether the sentence communicates a complete idea.

Numeracy

  • Re-establish number recognition, counting, comparison and patterns using objects children can handle. Practise matching quantities to numerals, grouping objects into bundles, comparing sets and extending simple patterns before moving to more complex calculations.
  • Teach addition and subtraction with concrete objects, drawings and number lines. Break each operation into small steps, provide repeated guided practice and check understanding through children’s explanations, with particular attention to subtraction and both levels of addition.
  • Use short, familiar Gondi word problems and act them out with objects. Teach children to identify the question, show the quantities, decide whether to add or subtract and explain the answer. Bring time, money, shapes and measurement into practical classroom activities.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Prioritise frequent classroom mentoring in Gondi schools where sentence reading, reading comprehension, sentence writing and number operations are weak. Demonstrate a complete lesson that links oral language to sentence reading and writing, and another that teaches number sense and operations with objects; review student work and track whether teachers use the strategies.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Ensure Gondi MLE schools receive regular CRCC support and the materials needed for foundational reading and hands-on numeracy. Review block-wise school evidence on number recognition, addition, subtraction, sentence reading and comprehension, and resolve administrative issues that interrupt teaching time or access to resources.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Treat the Gondi findings as a priority in district-level academic and administrative reviews. Require blocks to present school-level evidence of support to the lowest-performing competencies, follow up on gaps in teacher availability and materials, and coordinate the participation of DIET and language resource persons.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Take the academic lead in designing a Gondi catch-up approach that begins with number sense and sentence-level literacy. Develop graded Gondi sentence and passage materials, oral-to-written language activities, and concrete number-operation and word-problem tasks; train CRCCs and teachers to use them and review progress through classroom observations and student work.

Way Forward

Teachers should use the results to identify students who need extra support and to plan differentiated instruction. Schools and clusters can bring the performance-group data into Monthly Cluster Meetings and classroom observations, and use Sikhyana Sopan to track each student’s progress by competency. The State and districts can use the findings to focus teacher development, teaching-learning materials and classroom support on the weakest competencies. The purpose of grouping students is not to label them, but to understand what they can do, what they are yet to learn and what support will help them progress.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Ho, 408 children were assessed in 63 schools in Kendujhar. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 99% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 95% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 99% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 89% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 86% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 82% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 18% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 62% of the students in Ho correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 38% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 94% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 75% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 25% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 85% of the students scored above 75%.

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 93% of students in Ho were in the proficient group (L4), while 7% were in L0 to L3.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Ho

Decoding skills

In Ho, children demonstrate strong performance across most early literacy skills. Phonological awareness is 95%, oral reading fluency 93%, word reading accuracy (untimed) 86% and sentence reading 82%. Word writing is 94%, independent writing 85% and sentence writing 75%. These results suggest that most children can work with sounds, words and sentences and can express ideas in writing.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension are both 99%, and picture comprehension is 89%. Reading comprehension is lower at 62%, despite strong oral reading fluency and sentence reading. This suggests that children can read aloud and understand spoken language, but a proportion still need support to interpret, connect and respond to ideas in written text. The difference between independent writing (85%) and reading comprehension (62%) also suggests that written expression and reading for meaning may be developing at different rates.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include a classroom emphasis on accurate or fluent reading without enough time devoted to discussing meaning, asking inferential questions or connecting ideas across a passage. Children may be able to decode and read sentences but need more explicit teaching to monitor understanding, identify key information and explain what they have read. The strong oral language scores provide a strong foundation for this work.

15

Math in Ho

Foundational skills

Number sense is relatively strong, number identification is 81% untimed and 77% timed, number comparison is 80% and counting in bundles is 88%. Number patterns are lower at 61%. Addition Level 1 is 71% and Level 2 is 61%; Subtraction Level 1 is 56% and Level 2 is 60%. This indicates that number recognition and grouping are more secure than patterning and the two operations, particularly subtraction.

Application skills

Children perform well in multiplication (83%), measurement (87%), 2-D shape recognition (87%) and data handling (80%). Division is 68%, money 73%, time 52% and 3-D shape recognition 74%. Word problems are weaker: 49% score above 75% in addition word problems and 41% in subtraction word problems. The pattern suggests that children can manage several practical or recognisable mathematical tasks, but need more support to apply operations when they are embedded in a problem and to use time-related concepts.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include greater familiarity with concrete grouping, measurement and visual shapes than with number patterns, time and multi-step problem situations. Children may be practising multiplication or measurement as separate procedures but may not be consistently asked to explain the reasoning behind an operation or transfer it to a word problem. Time concepts often require repeated practical work with clocks, daily schedules and duration. The language and context of word problems may also affect performance and should be checked.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Maintain the strong sound, word and sentence-reading foundations through regular reading practice, while checking that children read accurately and understand what they are reading.
  • Make comprehension an instructional priority. Use short Ho passages and ask children to identify key details, retell events, explain reasons and answer factual and inferential questions. Encourage them to refer back to the text when answering.
  • Use children’s strong oral language and independent writing to deepen written expression and comprehension together. Ask them to discuss a passage, write a short response, explain a character or event, and support their answer with information from the text.

Numeracy

  • Build on strong counting in bundles and number comparison to teach number patterns and the relationship between addition and subtraction. Use objects, number cards and number lines, asking children to explain how they know what comes next or how a quantity changes.
  • Strengthen subtraction and consolidate both levels of addition and subtraction through concrete examples, drawings and guided practice. Ask children to explain their strategy and check answers using the inverse operation where appropriate.
  • Increase the use of Ho-contextualised word problems, Math vocabulary, and practical activities involving time, money and division. Act out problems, use real or model clocks and coins, and guide children to identify information, select an operation and explain their reasoning.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Use classroom visits to check whether teachers are moving from fluent reading to deeper comprehension and from routine calculations to problem-solving. Demonstrate text-based questioning and practical time/word-problem lessons, review student responses and give teachers specific feedback on how to extend learning beyond already strong competencies.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Ensure schools have regular academic support and practical materials such as graded Ho reading texts, clocks, calendars, play money and number resources. Review whether CRCCs are following up on reading comprehension, subtraction, word problems and time, and address school-level administrative barriers promptly.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Use district reviews to protect and extend Ho learning gains while focusing attention on comprehension and mathematical application. Ask blocks to report evidence from classroom visits and student work, and coordinate resources and administrative support for schools that need additional academic attention.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead an enrichment-and-consolidation plan for Ho schools. Develop comprehension-rich Ho reading materials and contextualised tasks for subtraction, word problems, time and division; orient teachers and CRCCs on strategies that deepen reasoning, and use demonstration lessons and student-work reviews to support consistent implementation.

Way Forward

The system should move from consolidating fluency and routine procedures to deepening comprehension, reasoning and problem-solving. Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should keep both strengths and gaps in view, reading results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to protect

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension (99%), phonological awareness (95%), word writing (94%), oral reading fluency (93%), counting in bundles (88%), measurement and 2-D shape recognition (87%) and multiplication (83%).

Gaps to close

Reading comprehension (62%), number patterns (61%), subtraction at Level 1 (56%) and Level 2 (60%), time (52%), division (68%), and word problems, where only 49% (addition) and 41% (subtraction) of children score above 75%.

Evidence to collect

Samples of children’s written responses to Ho passages, records of the strategies children use to solve and check subtraction and word problems, and observation notes from CRCC visits on how often teachers ask inferential and reasoning questions.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Juanga, 300 children were assessed in 48 schools in Kendujhar. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.
