STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 93% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 90% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 92% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 84% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 90% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 60% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 40% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 63% of the students in Juanga correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 37% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 80% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 59% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 41% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 72% of the students scored above 75%.

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 96% of students in Juanga were in the proficient group (L4), while 4% were in L0 to L3.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Juanga

Decoding skills

In Juanga, children show strong performance in phonological awareness (90%), oral reading fluency (96%), word reading accuracy (untimed) (90%) and word writing (80%). However, sentence reading is 60% and sentence writing is 59%, indicating a gap between reading or writing individual words and working with complete sentences. Independent writing is 72%, suggesting that many children can attempt to express ideas, but sentence construction is not yet secure for all.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (93%), listening comprehension (92%) and picture comprehension (84%) are strengths. Reading comprehension is 63%, which is lower than the oral-language and picture-comprehension results. This suggests that children understand spoken language and visual information more readily than they make meaning from written passages. The combination of relatively strong word reading and lower sentence reading and reading comprehension points to a need to strengthen the transition from decoding to understanding connected text.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include insufficient practice reading complete sentences and short passages, limited opportunities to discuss a text while reading, and a stronger emphasis on word-level reading than on meaning-making. Sentence writing may also be affected if children are not regularly supported to say a complete idea, arrange it into a sentence and then write it. Familiarity and availability of Juanga reading materials may influence how easily children connect oral language to print; this should be explored rather than assumed.

15

Math in Juanga

Foundational skills

Number recognition is 76% untimed and 78% timed, counting in bundles is 81%, while number comparison is 73% and number patterns 56%. Addition Level 1 is 65% and Level 2 is 53%; Subtraction Level 1 is 43% and Level 2 is 46%. This indicates that recognition and grouping are comparatively stronger, but number patterns and operations, especially subtraction, need attention.

Application skills

Children show strengths in multiplication (82%), measurement (85%), 2-D shape recognition (87%) and data handling (79%). Division is 59%, money 52%, time 39% and 3-D shape recognition 73%. Word problems are weak, with 33% scoring above 75% in addition and 27% in subtraction. This pattern suggests that children can perform some familiar or practical tasks, but have difficulty applying addition and subtraction in contextual situations and working with time.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited conceptual practice with subtraction, insufficient use of number patterns to build understanding of operations, and a lack of regular opportunities to act out and discuss word problems. Children may be more familiar with measurement, shapes and multiplication activities than with time and money tasks. The language used in word problems may also create an additional barrier if the context or mathematical vocabulary is unfamiliar.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Continue regular phonological-awareness and word-reading activities, but connect them to sentence reading. Use word cards to build meaningful Juanga sentences and practise reading them with expression and understanding.
  • Use familiar Juanga stories, pictures and short passages to strengthen reading comprehension. Ask children to predict, retell, sequence events and answer factual and inferential questions, linking what they hear and see to what they read.
  • Build sentence writing through oral rehearsal, shared writing and sentence frames. Ask children to describe familiar events or pictures, say a complete sentence, arrange the words and then write it independently.

Numeracy

  • Build number patterns and comparison through counting sequences, grouping and bundling objects. Ask children to explain patterns and connect changes in quantity to addition and subtraction.
  • Prioritise subtraction with concrete take-away and comparison activities, moving from objects to drawings and number sentences. Consolidate addition Level 1 and Level 2 while checking whether children understand the operation, not just the steps.
  • Teach addition and subtraction word problems through acted-out Juanga situations with Math vocabulary. Use objects, pictures and simple diagrams to identify what is known and what is being asked; also provide practical activities with clocks, money, division and measurement.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • During mentoring visits, focus on the transition from word reading to sentence reading and comprehension, and from number recognition to subtraction and word-problem solving. Demonstrate a Juanga shared-reading lesson and a concrete subtraction lesson, then review student work and agree on targeted follow-up with teachers.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Review school-level implementation of Juanga literacy and numeracy priorities in block meetings. Ensure access to Juanga reading resources and hands-on Math materials, monitor regular CRCC mentoring and address administrative constraints that reduce teaching time or interrupt academic support.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Include Juanga MLE schools in a regular district review of learning priorities, with specific follow-up on sentence reading, comprehension, subtraction and word problems. Hold blocks accountable for evidence of classroom support and coordinate timely resolution of resource and staffing issues.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Develop and lead a Juanga academic support package focused on sentence-level literacy, comprehension, subtraction and word problems. Work with language resource persons to prepare familiar texts and contextualised Math activities, orient teachers and CRCCs, and use demonstration classrooms to show effective practices.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should keep both strengths and gaps in view, reading results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to protect

Oral reading fluency (96%), oral vocabulary (93%), listening comprehension (92%), phonological awareness and word reading accuracy (both 90%), 2-D shape recognition (87%), measurement (85%) and multiplication (82%).

Gaps to close

Sentence reading (60%), sentence writing (59%), reading comprehension (63%), number patterns (56%), subtraction at Level 1 (43%) and Level 2 (46%), time (39%), money (52%), and word problems, where only 33% (addition) and 27% (subtraction) of children score above 75%.

Evidence to collect

Samples of sentences children read and write independently, their responses to short Juanga passages, the strategies they use for subtraction and word problems, and CRCC observation notes on the availability and use of Juanga reading materials.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Kisan, 202 children were assessed in 30 schools in Sambalpur. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 96% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 96% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 94% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 87% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 85% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 67% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 33% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 54% of the students in Kisan correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 46% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 77% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 57% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 43% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 86% of the students scored above 75%.

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 93% of students in Kisan were in the proficient group (L4), while 7% were in L0 to L3.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 88% of the students in Kisan counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 82% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 79% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 61% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 55% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 45% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 44% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 34% in subtraction word problems.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Kisan

Decoding skills

In Kisan, children demonstrate strong early literacy foundations: phonological awareness is 96%, oral reading fluency 93%, word reading accuracy (untimed) 85% and word writing 77%. Sentence reading is lower at 67%, indicating that the ability to read words fluently is not yet consistently translating into reading connected sentences. Independent writing is strong at 86%, while sentence writing is 57%, suggesting that children may be able to attempt open-ended writing but need further support to organise ideas into complete sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (96%), listening comprehension (94%) and picture comprehension (87%) are strong. Reading comprehension is 54%, the lowest literacy score, despite strong oral language and oral reading fluency. This indicates that children may understand spoken Kisan and visual prompts but find it harder to make meaning from written text. The difference between independent writing (86%) and sentence writing (57%) also suggests that children need support in structuring written ideas, even when they can generate content independently.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited guided practice in reading and discussing connected Kisan text, a focus on oral reading fluency without sufficient comprehension checks, and fewer opportunities to model how to build a complete sentence in writing. Children may benefit from explicit teaching that links oral narration, sentence construction, reading for meaning and written responses.

15

Math in Kisan

Foundational skills

Number sense is a relative strength, number identification is 82% untimed and 79% timed, number comparison is 79% and counting in bundles is 88%. Number patterns are lower at 58%. Addition Level 1 is 71% and Level 2 is 61%, while Subtraction Level 1 and Level 2 are 53% and 55%. This suggests that children are relatively comfortable recognising and grouping numbers, but need more support with patterns and with developing reliable addition and subtraction strategies.

Application skills

Children perform strongly in multiplication (82%), measurement (89%), 2-D shape recognition (92%), 3-D shape recognition (84%) and data handling (82%). Division is 57%, money 64% and time 43%. Word problems remain a major gap: 44% score above 75% in addition word problems and 34% in subtraction word problems. The pattern suggests that children can manage several practical or visual mathematical tasks, but have difficulty applying operations in contextual problems, particularly subtraction, and working with time.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include stronger exposure to concrete and visual tasks such as measurement and shapes than to time concepts or division; insufficient practice connecting number operations to everyday situations; and difficulty interpreting the language or identifying the operation in word problems. Lower number-pattern performance may also limit children's ability to notice relationships that support calculation strategies.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Use Kisan sound and word activities to maintain strong phonological awareness and word reading, while ensuring children regularly move from words to complete sentences and short passages.
  • Make reading comprehension a daily focus. Use short Kisan texts, ask children to retell and sequence events, locate information in the text and answer factual and inferential questions. Discuss the meaning of the text rather than treating fluent reading as the final goal.
  • Use children’s strong independent writing as a starting point for sentence writing. Have children orally explain an idea, organise it into a complete sentence, use sentence frames where needed and gradually write without support.

Numeracy

  • Build on strong number recognition and counting in bundles to strengthen number patterns. Use objects, number cards and simple sequences, asking children to explain what changes and predict the next number.
  • Consolidate addition and subtraction through concrete materials, drawings and number lines, with extra attention to subtraction. Ask children to show and explain their strategy, and provide practice across both levels before moving to word problems.
  • Use Kisan-contextualised word problems involving familiar daily activities. Act out addition and subtraction situations, guide children to identify the operation and explain their reasoning; include practical learning with clocks, money and division to address weaker application areas.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Mentor teachers to use strong oral language and independent writing as a bridge to reading comprehension and sentence writing, while also checking number patterns, subtraction and word-problem instruction. Demonstrate lessons, review children’s written responses and numeracy work, and follow up on agreed classroom changes during subsequent visits.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Ensure Kisan MLE schools have regular CRCC mentoring and access to graded Kisan reading materials and practical Math resources. Review school-level progress on reading comprehension, sentence writing, subtraction, word problems and time, and resolve administrative barriers to consistent classroom support.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Make Kisan learning priorities a standing item in district reviews. Require blocks to share evidence of classroom-level action and CRCC follow-up, and coordinate administrative support for teacher availability, materials and focused academic interventions in MLE schools.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead a Kisan-specific academic response that strengthens comprehension, sentence writing, number patterns, subtraction and word-problem solving. Work with Kisan language resource persons and teachers to develop familiar texts, sentence-writing supports and contextualised Math tasks, and build teacher and CRCC capacity through focused sessions and demonstration lessons.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should read results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to build on

Phonological awareness and oral vocabulary (both 96%), listening comprehension (94%), oral reading fluency (93%), 2-D shape recognition (92%), measurement (89%), counting in bundles (88%) and independent writing (86%).

Gaps to close

Reading comprehension (54%), sentence writing (57%), sentence reading (67%), number patterns (58%), subtraction (53% and 55%), time (43%), division (57%), money (64%), and word problems, where only 44% (addition) and 34% (subtraction) of children score above 75%.

Evidence to collect

Children’s retellings and written answers on short Kisan texts, samples showing how they turn spoken ideas into written sentences, their explanations of subtraction strategies and operation choices, and CRCC notes on follow-up of agreed classroom changes.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Koya, 327 children were assessed in 52 schools in Malkangiri. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to read the findings

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). Students are placed in five performance groups for each competency, L0 to L4, signifying increasing performance. For the Koya assessment, the results available for every competency are the share of students in L4 (scoring above 75%); the bars therefore show L4 in green and the remaining students (L0 to L3 together) in grey.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 95% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 79% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 87% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 79% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 63% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 57% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 43% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 46% of the students in Koya correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 54% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 69% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 53% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 47% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 71% of the students scored above 75%.

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 75% of students in Koya were in the proficient group (L4), while 25% were in L0 to L3.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 74% of the students in Koya counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 61% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 57% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

54% of the students discerned and completed more than three-quarters of the number patterns correctly.

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 43% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

Subtraction Level 2

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 42% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 58% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 32% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 28% in subtraction word problems.

14
Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Koya

Decoding skills

In Koya, children show stronger oral and sound foundations than connected-text reading. Phonological awareness is 79% and oral reading fluency is 75%, while word reading accuracy (untimed) is 63% and sentence reading is 57%. Word writing is 69% and sentence writing is 53%, indicating that many children need support to move from recognising and reading words to reading and writing complete sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (95%) and listening comprehension (87%) are relative strengths, and picture comprehension is 79%. Reading comprehension is much lower at 46%, while independent writing is 71%. This suggests that children can understand familiar spoken Koya and visual prompts better than they can independently make meaning from written text. The lower sentence-reading score may be contributing to the difficulty in reading comprehension. Independent writing is comparatively stronger than sentence writing, suggesting a need to support the organisation of ideas into complete sentences.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited exposure to short, graded Koya reading materials, insufficient guided practice with complete sentences, and classroom routines that may give more attention to oral responses and word reading than to discussing the meaning of a text. Children may need more opportunities to connect spoken Koya vocabulary with written sentences, retell what they read and explain their answers.

15

Math in Koya

Foundational skills

Number identification is 61% in the untimed task and 57% in the timed task. Number comparison (73%) and counting in bundles (74%) are somewhat stronger, while number patterns are 54%. Addition Level 1 is 50% and Level 2 is 43%; Subtraction Level 1 is 32% and Level 2 is 42%. This indicates that number recognition and grouping are still developing and that basic operations, particularly subtraction, need substantial support.

Application skills

Children show relative strengths in 2-D shape recognition and data handling (both 78%), measurement (74%), multiplication (68%) and division (67%). Performance is lower in 3-D shape recognition (65%), money (40%) and time (41%). Word problems are a major gap: 33% score above 75% in addition word problems and 28% in subtraction word problems. This suggests that children may manage some familiar or visual tasks but struggle to interpret a situation and decide which operation to use, especially in subtraction problems.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include gaps in number recognition and patterning that make operation learning harder, limited use of concrete materials to show grouping and taking away, and insufficient practice explaining how children chose an operation. Word-problem language may be unfamiliar or may place an additional comprehension demand on children. Lower performance in money and time may also reflect fewer opportunities to use coins, clocks and daily schedules as practical learning materials.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Use familiar Koya words for sound games, letter-sound work and repeated word reading, then guide children to read short, meaningful sentences rather than stopping at isolated words.
  • Use short Koya stories, pictures and oral discussion to build reading comprehension; ask children to retell events, sequence pictures and answer simple factual and inferential questions using clues from the text.
  • Build sentence writing through oral rehearsal, picture prompts and shared writing; help children say a complete idea, arrange the words into a sentence and then write it independently.

Numeracy

  • Strengthen number recognition, counting in bundles and number patterns with seeds, stones and sticks; ask children to group, compare and explain quantities before moving to written number work.
  • Give focused support in addition and especially subtraction using objects, drawings and number lines; move from taking away and comparing quantities to number sentences, and check that children can explain their strategy.
  • Use familiar Koya situations for addition and subtraction word problems with Math vocabulary; act out the problem, identify what is known and what is asked, choose the operation and explain the answer, while using real or model clocks and money for practical learning.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • During school visits, focus on whether teachers are moving from word reading to sentence meaning and from number practice to conceptual addition and subtraction. Demonstrate a Koya shared reading and retelling activity and a hands-on subtraction word problem, review children’s work and follow up on one agreed classroom change.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Review Koya MLE school progress on reading comprehension, sentence reading and writing, number patterns, subtraction and word problems in block meetings. Ensure teachers have Koya reading resources and hands-on Math materials, CRCC visits happen regularly and administrative barriers to classroom support are resolved.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Make Koya learning priorities part of district-level reviews and ask blocks to present school-level evidence from classroom visits, student work and CRCC mentoring. Coordinate timely support for teacher availability, learning materials and focused follow-up in schools where reading comprehension and basic operations remain weak.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead a Koya-specific academic response by working with language resource persons and teachers to prepare graded Koya texts, sentence-writing activities and contextualised number-operation and word-problem resources. Build teacher and CRCC capacity through focused demonstrations and review student work to refine the support.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should read results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to build on

Oral vocabulary (95%), listening comprehension (87%), phonological awareness and picture comprehension (both 79%), 2-D shape recognition and data handling (both 78%).

Gaps to close

Reading comprehension (46%), sentence writing (53%), sentence reading (57%), number identification (61% untimed, 57% timed), subtraction (32% and 42%), money (40%), time (41%), and word problems, where only 33% (addition) and 28% (subtraction) of children score above 75%.

Evidence to collect

Children’s retellings of short Koya texts, samples of sentences they write independently, their explanations of subtraction strategies and operation choices, and CRCC notes on the availability and use of graded Koya texts and concrete materials.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Kui, 339 children were assessed in 59 schools in Kandhamal and Kalahandi. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to read the findings

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). Students are placed in five performance groups for each competency, L0 to L4, signifying increasing performance. For the Kui assessment, the results available for every competency are the share of students in L4 (scoring above 75%); the bars therefore show L4 in green and the remaining students (L0 to L3 together) in grey.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 86% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 69% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 63% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 63% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 60% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 51% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 49% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 23% of the students in Kui correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 77% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 65% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 34% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 66% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 58% of the students scored above 75%.

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 68% of students in Kui were in the proficient group (L4), while 32% were in L0 to L3.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 66% of the students in Kui counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 54% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 57% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

26% of the students discerned and completed more than three-quarters of the number patterns correctly.

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 41% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

Subtraction Level 2

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 32% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 68% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 22% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 28% in subtraction word problems.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Kui

Decoding skills

In Kui children show emerging foundations in phonological awareness (69%) and oral reading fluency (68%), but word reading accuracy (untimed) is 60% and sentence reading is 51%. Word writing is 65%, while sentence writing is only 34%, indicating substantial difficulty in constructing complete written sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary is 86%, but listening comprehension (63%) and picture comprehension (63%) are lower. Reading comprehension is particularly weak at 23%, and independent writing is 58%. This suggests that understanding familiar words does not consistently translate into understanding spoken instructions, interpreting pictures or making meaning from written text. The very low reading-comprehension score, together with low sentence reading and sentence writing, points to a need for sustained support across connected reading, comprehension and written expression.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include limited practice with listening to and discussing longer words, insufficient access to familiar Kui texts, and a gap between word-level practice and reading connected sentences. Children may need teachers to model how to understand a sentence, use picture clues, retell information and express an idea orally before writing it. The language and familiarity of assessment prompts should also be checked, as comprehension tasks may be affected by unfamiliar vocabulary or context.

15

Math in Kui

Foundational skills

Number identification is 54% in the untimed task and 57% in the timed task. Number comparison is 59% and counting in bundles is 66%, while number patterns are only 26%. Addition Level 1 and Level 2 are 51% and 47%; Subtraction Level 1 and Level 2 are both 32%. This indicates that number recognition and grouping are still developing, number patterns are a significant gap, and children need intensive support to understand addition and subtraction.

Application skills

No application competency reaches 75% in this language. Data handling is 63%, 2-D shape recognition 55%, multiplication 47%, measurement 41%, 3-D shape recognition 48%, division 28%, money 33% and time 19%. Word problems are especially difficult, with 22% scoring above 75% in addition and 28% in subtraction. This broad pattern suggests that children need more opportunities to apply number concepts in practical situations and may struggle when a task requires them to interpret language, select an operation or use an unfamiliar representation.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include insecure number patterns and number relationships, limited opportunities to use concrete objects to explore operations, and too little guided practice moving from objects to drawings and number sentences. Word problems may be especially challenging when their wording or context is unfamiliar. Low time, money and division results may also reflect limited hands-on teaching with clocks, coins, sharing and grouping situations. Classroom observation and review of the exact assessment items are needed before identifying causes.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Rebuild early reading step by step through Kui sound games, letter-sound connections and familiar word reading, followed by teacher-led reading of short sentences; check that children understand each sentence they read.
  • Make listening and comprehension routines part of every lesson: tell or read a short Kui story, discuss key words and pictures, ask children to retell it and answer simple questions before asking them to read independently.
  • Teach sentence writing through oral expression, picture description, word cards and sentence frames; support children to say a complete idea, arrange the words and write a sentence, gradually reducing teacher support.

Numeracy

  • Prioritise number patterns, number recognition and counting in bundles using local objects and number cards; practise matching quantities to numerals, extending sequences and explaining what changes.
  • Teach addition and subtraction from the beginning with concrete objects and drawings, giving particular attention to subtraction; model each step, use number lines and check understanding through children’s explanations.
  • Use acted-out Kui word problems with Math vocabulary and practical stations for sharing, grouping, money and time; guide children to identify the question, represent quantities, choose an operation and explain their answer.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Provide frequent, demonstration-based mentoring in Kui schools, focusing on listening comprehension, sentence reading and writing, number patterns and basic operations. Model a short oral-to-reading lesson and a hands-on number lesson, review children’s responses with teachers and return to check whether the agreed strategies are being used.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Give Kui MLE schools close block-level follow-up because gaps are visible across both literacy and numeracy. Ensure regular teacher support, access to Kui reading materials and practical Math resources, and planned CRCC visits; resolve issues that interrupt teaching time or prevent use of materials.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Place Kui learning improvement on the district review agenda with clear follow-up from each block. Review evidence on reading comprehension, sentence writing, number patterns, subtraction and word problems, and coordinate administrative support and resource allocation for schools requiring intensive assistance.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead a foundational catch-up plan for Kui schools. Work with Kui language resource persons to prepare simple graded texts, listening and comprehension activities, sentence-writing supports and practical numeracy resources; orient teachers and CRCCs to teach these skills in small steps and monitor classroom implementation.

Way Forward

Strengths to build on

Oral vocabulary (86%), phonological awareness (69%), oral reading fluency (68%), counting in bundles (66%) and data handling (63%).

Gaps to close

Reading comprehension (23%), sentence writing (34%), number patterns (26%), subtraction (32%), time (19%), division (28%), money (33%), and word problems, where only 22% (addition) and 28% (subtraction) of children score above 75%. Track the share of L0 and L1 learners in each.

18

Allocate funds and resources wherever possible for targeted interventions
Hold regular review meetings with BEOs and CRCCs to track reading data monthly, especially for children in L0 and L1
Encourage recognition for schools showing progress

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Kuvi, 269 children were assessed in 50 schools in Rayagada. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 94% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 76% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 82% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 75% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 48% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 41% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 59% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 42% of the students in Kuvi correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 58% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 60% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 48% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 52% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 65% of the students scored above 75%.

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 73% of students in Kuvi were in the proficient group (L4), while 27% were in L0 to L3.
