Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Kuvi

Decoding skills

In Kuvi, children show stronger oral language than decoding and connected-text reading. Phonological awareness is 76%, oral reading fluency is 73%, but word reading accuracy (untimed) is 48% and sentence reading is 41%. Word writing is 60% and sentence writing is 48%, indicating that many children need support with accurate word recognition and constructing complete sentences.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary (94%) and listening comprehension (82%) are strengths, while picture comprehension is 75%. Reading comprehension is 42%, and independent writing is 65%. This suggests that children understand spoken Kuvi better than they can independently read and interpret written text. The low word-reading accuracy and sentence-reading scores may be limiting reading comprehension, while the gap between oral language and written expression points to a need to connect discussion, reading and writing more deliberately.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include insufficient guided practice in accurate word reading, limited opportunities to read connected Kuvi sentences and short passages, and classroom emphasis on oral responses without enough follow-through into print. Children may need more explicit modelling of how to sound out or recognise words, read a sentence smoothly and check whether it makes sense.

15

Math in Kuvi

Foundational skills

Number identification is 63% in the untimed task and 51% in the timed task; number comparison is 63%, counting in bundles 75% and number patterns 42%. Addition Level 1 is 61% and Level 2 is 52%; Subtraction Level 1 and Level 2 are 46% and 45%. This suggests that children can work with bundles and some number tasks but need stronger number-pattern understanding and more secure addition and subtraction strategies. The difference between untimed and timed number identification may indicate that children recognise numbers but do not do so quickly and consistently.

Application skills

Children show a relative strength in 2-D shape recognition (75%) and data handling (71%). Measurement is 62%, multiplication 63%, division 50%, money 41%, time 38% and 3-D shape recognition 59%. Word problems are particularly weak: 23% score above 75% in addition and 30% in subtraction. This suggests that children may be more comfortable with familiar visual tasks such as shapes and data than with interpreting a problem and selecting an operation, particularly in addition word problems.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include uneven number recognition fluency, limited work with number patterns and insufficient concrete practice of addition and subtraction. Children may be familiar with measurement through everyday activities but have fewer structured opportunities to use clocks, money and 3-D objects. Word-problem performance may also be affected by unfamiliar language or contexts and limited modelling of how to represent a problem before calculating.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Strengthen accurate word reading with Kuvi sound-letter activities, familiar word cards and teacher modelling; use repeated reading to build accuracy before expecting children to read longer sentences independently.
  • Use oral vocabulary and listening strengths to support comprehension: discuss a picture or short Kuvi story, introduce key words, read together and ask children to retell and answer questions using the text.
  • Build sentence reading and writing together through shared reading, sentence strips and picture prompts; ask children to read a complete sentence, explain its meaning and then write a related sentence of their own.

Numeracy

  • Practise number identification in both untimed and timed activities, alongside counting in bundles, comparison and number patterns; use objects and number cards so children can explain the number relationships they notice.
  • Teach addition and subtraction with concrete materials, drawings and number lines, giving regular practice across both levels and checking that children understand the meaning of each operation.
  • Use familiar Kuvi situations to teach word problems with Math vocabulary, money and time; act out the problem, represent it with objects or drawings, decide which operation is needed and explain the answer, while extending practical measurement work.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • During mentoring visits, focus on accurate word reading, sentence comprehension and the transition from oral language to print, alongside number-pattern and operation teaching. Demonstrate a Kuvi guided-reading lesson and a word-problem lesson, examine student responses and provide teachers with one specific next step.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Ensure Kuvi schools receive regular CRCC mentoring and have access to suitable Kuvi reading materials and hands-on numeracy resources. Review block-level evidence on word reading, sentence reading, number patterns and word problems, and resolve administrative barriers to regular classroom support.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Use district reviews to ensure that Kuvi schools receive targeted support for reading accuracy, comprehension, addition, subtraction and word problems. Ask blocks to share evidence from school visits and student work, and coordinate resource and staffing support where implementation gaps are identified.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Develop a Kuvi-focused academic support plan with language resource persons and teachers. Prepare familiar graded reading texts, word-reading and sentence activities, and practical number-operation and word-problem resources; strengthen teacher and CRCC capacity through demonstration lessons and review of student work.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should read results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to build on

Oral vocabulary (94%), listening comprehension (82%), phonological awareness (76%), and counting in bundles and 2-D shape recognition (both 75%).

Gaps to close

Sentence reading (41%), reading comprehension (42%), word reading accuracy and sentence writing (both 48%), number patterns (42%), timed number identification (51%), subtraction (46% and 45%), time (38%), money (41%), and word problems, where only 23% (addition) and 30% (subtraction) of children score above 75%.

Evidence to collect

Running records of children’s word and sentence reading accuracy, their retellings of short Kuvi texts, samples of independently written sentences, and how they represent word problems before calculating.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Mundari, 342 children were assessed in 56 schools in Mayurbhanj and Sundargarh. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to read the findings

The findings are presented in bar graphs, where each row represents one competency (such as listening comprehension or sentence reading). Students are placed in five performance groups for each competency, L0 to L4, signifying increasing performance. For the Mundari assessment, the results available for every competency are the share of students in L4 (scoring above 75%); the bars therefore show L4 in green and the remaining students (L0 to L3 together) in grey.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 100% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 97% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 100% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 90% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 80% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 77% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 23% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 69% of the students in Mundari correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 31% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 79% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 67% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 33% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 82% of the students scored above 75%.

12

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 92% of students in Mundari were in the proficient group (L4), while 8% were in L0 to L3.

Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Mundari

Decoding skills

In Mundari, children show strong decoding foundations. Phonological awareness is 97%, oral reading fluency 92%, word reading accuracy (untimed) 80% and sentence reading 77%. Word writing is 79%, while sentence writing is 67%. This indicates that many children can read words and sentences and write words, but sentence-level written expression remains an area to strengthen. The scorecard does not report separate scores for letter-naming fluency or word-reading fluency; oral reading fluency is the available timed reading indicator.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension are both 100%, and picture comprehension is 90%. Reading comprehension is lower at 69%, while independent writing is 82%. The pattern suggests that children have very strong oral language and can understand pictures, but some still need support to interpret written passages and express their understanding in complete written sentences. Sentence writing (67%) is lower than independent writing, indicating that the structure and completeness of written responses may need attention.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include reading lessons that focus on fluency and correct reading but provide fewer opportunities to discuss deeper meaning, make inferences or support answers with evidence from a text. Children may also need more explicit modelling of how to turn an oral idea into a well-formed written sentence. Since the scores are relatively strong overall, the next step may be to strengthen depth and consistency. These are hypotheses to verify in classrooms.

15

Math in Mundari

Foundational skills

Number identification is 92% untimed and 88% timed, number comparison 89%, counting in bundles 95% and number patterns 79%. Addition Level 1 is 89% and Level 2 is 76%; Subtraction Level 1 is 74% and Level 2 is 73%. This is a strong foundational profile, with subtraction comparatively lower than addition and number sense. The scores suggest that most children have developed many core number skills, while a group still needs support to consolidate subtraction and more complex operations. The scorecard does not separately report timed and untimed accuracy/fluency for addition and subtraction.

Application skills

Children show strengths in measurement (93%), 2-D shape recognition (91%), data handling (89%), multiplication (88%), 3-D shape recognition (84%) and division (76%). Money is 72% and time 55%. Word problems are weaker: 52% score above 75% in addition and 45% in subtraction. This suggests that children can handle many practical and operational tasks but need more support to apply subtraction in contextual problems and to understand time-related concepts.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors include greater familiarity with concrete measurement, shapes and grouping activities than with time concepts and contextual subtraction problems. Children may know how to carry out an operation but need more practice identifying when and why to use it in a story or everyday situation. Time concepts require repeated practical work with clocks, calendars, duration and daily routines. These are possibilities to test through classroom tasks and student explanations.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Maintain strong phonological awareness, word reading and sentence reading through regular Mundari reading, while adding questions that check meaning, inference and explanation rather than fluency alone.
  • Use short Mundari passages for deeper comprehension: ask children to identify key ideas, explain why something happened, retell in sequence and support answers with information from the text.
  • Strengthen sentence writing by modelling complete sentences, shared writing and short written responses to stories or familiar experiences; help children organise their ideas and check whether each sentence communicates a complete thought.

Numeracy

  • Consolidate strong number sense through activities that extend number patterns and require children to explain relationships, compare strategies and work with larger or less familiar quantities.
  • Focus additional practice on subtraction and Level 2 operations using drawings, number lines and practical situations; ask children to show their method and check their answer using addition where appropriate.
  • Strengthen application through Mundari-contextualised addition and subtraction word problems with Math vocabulary, especially subtraction; use clocks, calendars and daily schedules to build time concepts and ask children to explain their reasoning.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Use mentoring visits to move classroom practice from strong routine performance towards deeper comprehension, sentence writing and mathematical reasoning. Demonstrate a text-discussion lesson and a contextual subtraction/time lesson, review student explanations and written work, and support teachers to extend learning for children already meeting foundational expectations.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Enhance the learning profile in Mundari schools by ensuring regular CRCC mentoring, access to graded texts and Math materials, and follow-up on the remaining gaps in reading comprehension, sentence writing, subtraction word problems and time. Review school evidence in block meetings and resolve administrative barriers quickly.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Use district reviews to recognise and sustain Mundari strengths while ensuring targeted support for the remaining gaps. Ask blocks to present evidence of classroom-level work on comprehension, sentence writing, subtraction word problems and time, and coordinate any required administrative or resource support.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead an enrichment and consolidation strategy for Mundari schools. Develop comprehension-rich texts, sentence-writing tasks and contextual subtraction and time activities; support teachers and CRCCs to deepen learning through training and demonstration lessons, and use student work to identify where further extension is needed.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should read results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to protect

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension (both 100%), phonological awareness (97%), counting in bundles (95%), measurement (93%), number identification and oral reading fluency (both 92%), and 2-D shape recognition (91%).

Gaps to close

Time (55%), word problems, where 52% (addition) and 45% (subtraction) of children score above 75%, sentence writing (67%), reading comprehension (69%), money (72%) and subtraction (74% and 73%).

Data to add

Separate letter-naming and word-reading fluency scores, and timed and untimed results for addition and subtraction, would give a fuller picture of where children need consolidation.

PREFACE

Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) has been the state’s prime focus. On 5 September 2024, the state launched the NIPUN Odisha Mission, realigning its strategy with the NIPUN Bharat Mission for focused efforts to improve FLN levels up to Class 3.

Since 2007–08, Odisha has run a Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) programme for tribal and indigenous children in 1,317 schools across 17 districts, using 21 tribal languages. Having established the Odia baseline in 2024–25, the state extended the assessment in 2025–26 to 11 tribal languages alongside Odia.

The study used cluster randomised sampling, with MLE schools as clusters, stratified by language and then by district. Literacy and numeracy experts designed FLN competency-based tools for Class 3 on end-of-Class 2 competencies, with technical support from Central Square Foundation. The tools were finalised in Odia and then translated or transcreated into each tribal language by language experts. In July, 22 Master Trainers field-tested the language tools over two days with ten students per language across nine districts to establish their reliability and validity, and the observations from this pilot shaped the final tools. Data was collected one-on-one using Tangerine, a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) tool that captures responses on a mobile or tablet.

Across the 11 tribal languages, assessors tested 3,120 Class 3 children in 499 MLE schools during the 3rd week of August and 1st week of September, following robust quality control procedures. In Santali, 370 children were assessed in 60 schools in Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar. Protocols for data cleaning were followed and the data was checked for reliability before analysis. Experts within and outside the state were engaged to ensure rigour in the analysis and to articulate relevant recommendations for the way forward.

Two kinds of reports were generated for the language-wise study:

Detailed report for the state: elaborates on the study design and methodology, an overview of the skills assessed, findings, data reliability measures, limitations and recommendations for the way forward.

Language reports for all 11 tribal languages: these reports present students’ performance on the skills assessed in Class 3, language-wise.

The study was geared towards informing the way forward on enabling foundational learning in the state’s MLE schools. As the next step, dissemination, goal setting and planning to improve student learning will be undertaken at the state, district and sub-district levels.

STUDY BACKGROUND

Odisha's Commitment to Foundational Literacy and Numeracy

Odisha has taken a significant step towards foundational learning for all children by launching the NIPUN Odisha Mission in September 2024 under the leadership of the Honourable Chief Minister Shri Mohan Charan Majhi. The mission aims to ensure that all students in government schools, from Sishu Vatika (pre-primary) to Class 3, attain Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) competencies. NIPUN Odisha emphasises activity-based and play-based learning methodologies and teacher capacity-building to foster an engaging and effective learning environment for young children.

The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 highlights FLN as the cornerstone of all future learning. It underscores that the ability to "learn to read" by the end of Class 3 is essential for children to be able to "read to learn", and declares FLN an "urgent and necessary" priority (Ministry of Education 2020). In line with this vision, the Government of India launched the NIPUN Bharat Mission to ensure every child attains FLN by 2026–27 (Ministry of Education 2021).

Role of the Language-wise FLN Assessment

The NIPUN Odisha Language-wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (LFA) plays a pivotal role in setting learning goals and measuring the outcomes of the NIPUN Odisha Mission in each language of instruction. By assessing Class 3 students on end-of-Class 2 competencies, the study captures learning levels at the right time, allowing teachers and the system to identify children falling behind and the areas requiring focused intervention. While the PARAKH Survey assesses children at the end of Class 3, the LFA results provide a progress checkpoint to ensure readiness for achieving the NIPUN benchmark by the end of Class 3.

The mission aims to establish SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) goals so that every student achieves grade-level reading, writing and numeracy competencies by the end of Class 3, in all government and government-aided schools in the state.

2

Objective of the Language Wise Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment

In the 2024–25 assessment cycle, the state established the baseline learning levels for the mission in Odia. In 2025–26, the study was conducted in 11 tribal languages (Santali, Kisan, Mundari, Ho, Juanga, Koya, Bonda, Didayi, Gondi, Kui and Kuvi) along with Odia, to assess the current learning levels of Class 3 children in different competencies. The assessment will also help the state redesign interventions based on the evidence. It has the following objectives:

  1. Understand the current FLN learning levels of students in the 12 languages listed above, particularly in Class 3.
  2. Set targets at the state and district levels in each language to achieve grade-level competencies at the foundational level.
  3. Compare the learning of MLE school children with non-MLE school children in different numeracy and literacy competencies in selected MLE districts.
  4. Use the assessment data to guide state and district programme planning, including academic inputs such as materials, training and classroom support, and administrative inputs such as better review and monitoring.

STUDY DESIGN

Overview of the FLN Competencies Assessed in the Survey

Both the literacy and numeracy assessments included a mix of early foundational competencies and grade-appropriate skills that are essential for further learning. Without these core skills, students often struggle to progress through the curriculum. The assessments comprised two types of questions: timed and untimed.

  • Accuracy task: untimed questions measured accuracy, a student's ability to perform a task correctly, regardless of the time taken. In language, this might involve identifying the correct letter sound or reading a word correctly; in Math, it could involve solving a basic addition problem without errors. Accuracy reflects conceptual understanding and correctness of response.
  • Fluency task: timed questions assessed fluency, the speed and ease with which a student performs a task, within a fixed 60-second window, giving insight into the student's automaticity and comfort with the skill.

To ensure a natural assessment environment, students were not told whether a question was timed or untimed.

How to interpret:

In this example, 14% of students can read a grade-level story aloud correctly and fluently within a minute, but nearly one-third (27%) could not read a single word correctly. Fluency is critical for reading comprehension: it lets students move beyond decoding individual words to constructing meaning from connected text. Unless students can string words accurately and fluently into sentences, and sentences into coherent passages, they will struggle to comprehend what they read.

Literacy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Oral Vocabulary

On the Oral Vocabulary task, 100% of the students were proficient and could correctly identify more than seven out of ten everyday pictures, objects and actions.

Phonological Awareness

On the Phonological Awareness task, where students identified the initial sounds of grade-level words, 98% of the students were proficient and could identify the initial sounds of more than seven out of ten words.

Listening Comprehension

On the Listening Comprehension task, 100% of the students were proficient and correctly answered more than three out of five questions about a story read aloud to them.

Picture Comprehension

On this task, 97% of the students were proficient and answered more than 75% of the factual and inferential questions about a composite picture correctly.

Word Reading Untimed

On this task, 89% of the students were proficient and correctly read more than three-quarters of the frequently occurring words presented.

Sentence Reading

On the Sentence Reading task, 83% of the students read more than three out of five simple sentences of three or four words correctly, while 17% scored 75% or below.

Reading Comprehension

On the Reading Comprehension task, 76% of the students in Santali correctly answered more than three out of five questions on a simple passage, while 24% scored 75% or below. The passage had three factual and two inferential questions.

Word Writing

On the word writing task, assessed through dictation of familiar words, 86% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three words correctly.

Sentence Writing

On the sentence writing task, assessed through dictation of simple sentences of three or four words, 70% of the students were proficient and wrote more than three sentences correctly, while 30% scored 75% or below.

Independent Writing

On the independent writing task, where the child looked at two pictures and wrote about them independently, 82% of the students scored above 75%.

12

Literacy Findings: Fluency Tasks

Oral Reading Fluency

On the Oral Reading Fluency task, using a simple short story of five sentences, 94% of students in Santali were in the proficient group (L4), while 6% were in L0 to L3.

Letter Naming and Word Reading Timed

These timed tasks were administered, but the Santali report does not give separate results for them.

Numeracy Findings: Accuracy Tasks

Counting in Bundles

On this task, 99% of the students in Santali counted the bundles and answered conceptual questions correctly for more than three out of five questions.

Number Identification

On this task, students identified single and double-digit numbers using a table. 96% of the students correctly identified more than seven out of ten numbers, and 90% were proficient on the timed task.

Number Pattern

83% of the students discerned and completed more than three-quarters of the number patterns correctly.

Addition Level 2

On this task, students solved six addition problems, including one with carry over. 80% of students correctly solved more than four questions.

Subtraction Level 2

On this task, students solved subtraction problems, including borrowing. 79% of students correctly solved more than 75% of the questions, while 21% scored 75% or below.

Word Problems

When asked to solve word problems read aloud to them, 67% of students were proficient in addition word problems and 61% in subtraction word problems.

14
Interpretation of Findings

Literacy in Santali

Decoding skills

In Santali, children show strong performance across early decoding skills. Phonological awareness is 98%, oral reading fluency 94%, word reading accuracy (untimed) 89% and sentence reading 83%. Word writing is 86%, while sentence writing is 70%. This suggests that most children have developed strong sound, word and sentence-reading foundations, while sentence-level written expression remains a relative area for improvement.

Comprehension skills

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension are both 100%, and picture comprehension is 97%. Reading comprehension is 76%, while independent writing is 82%. These are strong results overall, although reading comprehension and sentence writing are lower than the oral-language and picture-comprehension scores. This suggests that children understand spoken and visual information very well, but some may need further support to interpret written passages deeply and express ideas in complete written sentences.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors to the remaining gap may include greater classroom emphasis on oral language, picture-based discussion and fluent reading than on deeper text interpretation, inference and evidence-based responses. Sentence writing may require more explicit modelling and opportunities to organise ideas into connected written responses.

15

Math in Santali

Foundational skills

Number identification is 96% untimed and 90% timed, number comparison 96%, counting in bundles 99% and number patterns 83%. Addition Level 1 is 83% and Level 2 is 80%; Subtraction Level 1 is 75% and Level 2 is 79%. This indicates a strong foundation in number sense and operations, with most children meeting the 75% benchmark across these competencies. The focus should be on ensuring consistency, explaining strategies and extending children’s reasoning rather than reteaching all foundational skills.

Application skills

Children show strong performance in multiplication (94%), division (84%), measurement (97%), money (85%), 2-D shape recognition (96%), 3-D shape recognition (97%) and data handling (95%). Time is comparatively lower at 52%. Word problems are also lower than other numeracy competencies: 67% score above 75% in addition and 61% in subtraction. This suggests that children are able to perform many mathematical operations and practical tasks, but need more opportunities to apply these skills to contextual problems and strengthen understanding of time.

Overall interpretation

Possible contributors to the remaining gaps include less frequent use of clocks, calendars and duration-based activities, and a need for more practice interpreting multi-step or story-based mathematical situations. Even where children can perform operations, they may need support to identify the relevant information and explain why an operation is appropriate.

16
Recommendations

The recommendations span five stakeholder groups. Teachers lead classroom improvement, while academic and administrative structures support them.

Teachers: strengthen classroom instruction

Literacy

  • Continue regular Santali sound, word and sentence-reading activities to sustain strong decoding, while including varied texts and opportunities for children to read independently.
  • Deepen reading comprehension through questions that require children to explain, infer, compare and justify answers using evidence from Santali texts, rather than relying only on recall or picture clues.
  • Build on strong independent and word writing to strengthen sentence writing; model complete sentences, ask children to write explanations or summaries and provide opportunities to revise and improve their written expression.

Numeracy

  • Maintain strong number sense through tasks that require children to explain number patterns, compare strategies and solve problems using different representations rather than only repeating familiar exercises.
  • Consolidate addition and subtraction across both levels, using children’s existing skills to introduce reasoning, estimation and checking strategies; include opportunities to explain and compare methods.
  • Give additional practical attention to time and contextual word problems with Math vocabulary, using clocks, calendars, timetables and familiar Santali situations; ask children to identify information, choose an operation and explain their solution.
CRCC (mentor): strengthen on-site teacher support
  • Use classroom visits to ensure strong Santali literacy and numeracy results are translating into deeper comprehension, sentence writing and problem-solving. Demonstrate text-based inference and explanation activities, alongside practical time and word-problem tasks, and help teachers plan extension for children who have already mastered foundational skills.
17
Block Education Office: provide close administrative support
  • Ensure schools sustain regular classroom teaching and mentoring while providing clocks, calendars, graded Santali texts and other resources needed for extension. Review school-level evidence on sentence writing, reading comprehension, time and word problems in block meetings and address any gaps in CRCC follow-up or material access.
District Education Office: drive district-level accountability
  • Use district-level reviews to protect the strong Santali learning profile and focus administrative attention on the remaining gaps in sentence writing, reading comprehension, time and word problems. Ask blocks to report evidence of classroom practice and ensure resources and academic support reach schools where needed.
DIET: provide academic leadership
  • Lead an enrichment-focused academic plan for Santali schools. Develop higher-order comprehension tasks, sentence-writing and short-response activities, contextual word problems and practical time resources; orient teachers and CRCCs to deepen reasoning and use student work to identify children who need consolidation or extension.

Way Forward

Progress reviews at school, cluster, block and district level should read results competency-wise and alongside the share of children in each performance group (L0 to L4).

Strengths to protect

Oral vocabulary and listening comprehension (both 100%), phonological awareness (98%), measurement and 3-D shape recognition (both 97%), number comparison and 2-D shape recognition (both 96%), and multiplication (94%).

Gaps to close

Time (52%), word problems, where 67% (addition) and 61% (subtraction) of children score above 75%, sentence writing (70%), reading comprehension (76%) and Level 1 subtraction (75%), which sits right at the benchmark.

Evidence to collect

Children’s written answers to inferential questions on Santali texts, samples of their summaries and explanations, their reasoning on time and story-based problems, and the share of children receiving extension rather than consolidation work.

18
